newsitem.title: USA: FTC to meet on Staples merger Monday.
newsitem.headline: FTC to meet on Staples merger Monday.

text.p: The Federal Trade Commission reaches a moment of truth Monday in the months-long effort by office superstore Staples to merge with rival Office Depot.

The FTC has announced it will hold a private meeting Monday, at which sources say the commission will take up the question of whether to approve the merger or seek a federal court injunction to halt it as anticompetitive under the nation's anti-trust laws.
The two office superstore chains announced in September they would merge, creating a company with more than 1,117 stores in the United States and annual revenues of more than $10 billion.
But much of the FTC staff is said to firmly oppose that merger, contending it would narrow competition from three office superstores to two, leaving competition from only OfficeMax.

The FTC staff appears to reject the argument by Staples and Office Depot that they are a small part of a broad market for computers, office supplies, office furniture and other equipment used by business.
Some of the documents supplied to the FTC have given staff members ammunition to make their case, although Staples and Office Depot have argued the documents are beside the point.
If the five-member FTC agrees with the staff, it will vote to take the case to federal court and seek an injunction against the merger. In the past such votes have often been split three-to-two.
Once the FTC acts it will take the case to court by a March 13 deadline, unless Office Depot and Staples choose to extend the deadline and continue negotiations with the government.

If the stores choose not to extend the deadline, the government would ask a federal judge to grant a temporary restraining order against the deal. Weeks later, after both sides made their cases, the judge would choose whether to grant a permanent injunction against the deal.
Under such circumstances, Office Depot and Staples would have to decide whether to commit significant resources to fighting a long and expensive court battle.
In the meantime, they would face the prospect of losing ground against the competition. In the past, a restraining order by a judge has often resulted in companies giving up a proposed merger.
